extracted.intended_audience: distance-education administrators, instructional designers, online instructors, and call-centre managers in educational institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for effective teaching presence in online learning and for designing/operating call centres in distance education (including strategic alignment, staffing, KM/CRM, and service models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three components of teaching presence
rubrics_metrics.description: The three critical components of teaching presence are design and organization, facilitating discourse, and direct instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These components remain critical in both online learning and classroom instruction; they form the broad theoretical model for maximizing teaching effectiveness rather than providing a cookbook of do's and don'ts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical/andragogical understanding and activity repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers must be equipped with a pedagogical (or andragogical) understanding of the learning process and have a set of learning activities at their disposal to orchestrate, motivate, and assess effective learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes conceptual grounding and a toolkit of activities rather than rote procedures; supports design and organization component of teaching presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical competence and internet efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Online teachers must have sufficient technical skill to navigate and contribute effectively within the online learning context, access necessary hardware, and possess internet efficacy (a personal sense of competence and comfort in the environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes basic troubleshooting skills so technical issues do not incapacitate the teacher; does not require being a technical expert but requires functional competence to handle inevitable technical challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resilience, innovativeness, and perseverance
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective online teachers must demonstrate the resilience, innovativeness, and perseverance typical of pioneers in unfamiliar technological and pedagogical terrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies during periods of rapid technological and pedagogical change (e.g., emergence of Semantic Web, Web 2.0); a disposition criterion rather than a discrete technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic alignment of call centre objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives established for a call centre must support and enhance the organisation’s strategic direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a call-routing centre suits needs for short answers/high volume, whereas organisations focused on customer loyalty need richer interactions; design should be chosen to achieve organisational goals rather than blindly matching industry benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of call-centre function to institutional mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Call-centre design and operating mode should match the institution's mission and intended contribution (e.g., routing, marketing, student retention, advising).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What fits one organisation will not fit all; examine what the organisation is trying to achieve and build processes/systems accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance productivity and quality; standardization vs customization
rubrics_metrics.description: Call centres must balance productivity (efficiency, standardization) and quality (customized service), managing the tension between standardisation and customization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmarking numbers may be misleading; high-volume standardised operations often yield low customer satisfaction—design choices should weigh trade-offs relevant to institutional goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outsourcing risk assessment for educational call centres
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding to outsource, assess complexity of managing relationships and the risk to the institution's teaching team and student relationship management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outsourcing may provide efficiency but carries risk because CSRs in education are part of the teaching team and relationship management; the loss of institutional connection can be costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mass-production call-centre anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise and avoid characteristics commonly criticised in call centres: low-skilled work; poor working conditions; fast, machine pacing of work; routine, standardized, and boring tasks; high stress; short, fast job cycles; poor job security; low pay; extreme employee monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These traits are typical of low-value, high-volume centres (telemarketing, surveying) and should be mitigated where the goal is quality service or educational support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional service model criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: In the professional service model technology complements rather than replaces labour; employees are educated and highly skilled; collaborative decision making, discretion, teamwork, firm-specific social capital and trust are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model supports high-value, skilled work and is intended to overcome the standard criticisms of call centres by enriching job content and relying on high-commitment HR practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass-customization model criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass customization model is a hybrid aiming to keep costs down while providing customised, high-quality interactive service through automation and process reengineering; requires CSRs to exercise discretion and skill in handling relatively complex interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automation helps lower cost, but human discretion is still required; this model tries to balance cost-control with service quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-involvement/collaborative structures and HR practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative structures and high-commitment human resource management practices improve service and job satisfaction; technology should complement labour and allow task variety and discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborative structures generally provide better service and are consistent with models that seek to increase employee satisfaction and user satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call-centre primary functions to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Call centres have particular significance in: (1) customer/student service and retention, (2) direct marketing, and (3) management information and student/customer feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a call centre, consider which of these functions it is intended to serve and design capabilities accordingly (e.g., advising, marketing, data collection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidated call-centre/help-desk one-stop capability
rubrics_metrics.description: A consolidated call centre/help desk in education should combine help-desk diagnostic skills with directive/prepared services of a typical call centre to provide one-stop support for both technical and content-related questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires a layered/tiered structure, access to a knowledge base, and availability of specialists for complex issues; front-line staff need communication, student-service experience, and adaptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered support model (Tier 0–3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Help desks/call centres are organised in tiers: Tier 0 (web-based self-help), Tier 1 (front-line facilitator), Tier 2 (desktop/technical analyst), Tier 3 (network/academic specialists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop web-based self-help (Tier 0) to reduce load and cost; escalate more complex issues through tiers; clearly document responsibilities and routing rules for each tier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-help and FAQ emphasis to reduce call volume
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive FAQ files and web-based self-help (Tier 0) should be developed because many calls (estimated ~86%) can be resolved automatically without human intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing automated self-help can reduce call volumes and improve user satisfaction; invest in good documentation and self-service interfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic skills and knowledge-base design
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge base for diagnostic questions must include step-by-step guides for asking diagnostic questions and solving problems, distinct from simple Q&A knowledge bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic skill is a learned capability; build knowledge bases that support decision trees and troubleshooting flows for Tier 1/2 staff and provide specialist escalation paths as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use CRM data for management information and instructional improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: CRM software should track contacts and accumulate information about courses and inquiries; this data should be analysed to inform instructional design, identify problematic course content, and guide remedial materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CRM tracking provides systematic, scalable feedback (reducing recency bias) useful to faculty and instructional designers in distributed delivery environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge management practices for customer-service effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Good knowledge management (KM) involves capturing relevant information, organizing and analyzing it, and making accurate, consistent information readily accessible to agents and customers via self-service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KM increases first-contact resolution, agent efficiency, and the ability to handle diverse/difficult calls; invest in organizing, analysing, and surfacing knowledge for agents and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call-centre consolidation criteria and optimal sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidation can yield economies of scale, reduced equipment costs, simplified tech rollout, better quality control, and reduced management; subunit/team optimal size is roughly ~50 agents for efficiency gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation should be considered when tasks/services overlap; beware diminishing returns above certain sizes and ensure consolidation aligns with service goals and KM capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segmentation and routing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern segmentation strategies route based on client value and service needs (e.g., low-value customers to self-service, high-value customers to high-touch service); in education, segmentation should be based on student characteristics and query type rather than commercial 'value' labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CRM and KM data to determine routing rules; segment by student level, area of study, or query complexity, and route many routine queries to self-service while routing specialized queries to trained agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase task variety to improve job and user satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Design jobs to increase task variety (mix administrative and other work), introduce high-commitment HR practices, and incorporate technology that complements labour to improve employee and user satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher task variety and skills requirements can increase job satisfaction and service quality; use training, KM, and role design to broaden agent responsibilities where appropriate.
